title: Microsoft Fabric security fundamentals
summary: Vendor architectural overview of Fabric's security model aimed at admins: how the SaaS platform separates metadata and compute, how authentication and authorization flow through Microsoft Entra ID and signed tokens, how data residency and multi-geo work, and how data is protected at rest and in transit.
audience: Fabric administrators, security administrators, network administrators, and workspace/database administrators evaluating or hardening a Fabric tenant.
why_it_matters: It supplies the platform-level security model an architecture-implementation knowledge base needs before any capability-specific security topic (OneLake, workspace roles) can be reasoned about — specifically the separation of the metadata platform from the back-end capacity platform, and how authorization is resolved and cached via signed tokens.
takeaways: Fabric is SaaS-first: platform security, compliance, and governance are largely built in rather than something admins must independently stand up, unlike traditional PaaS data platforms.
Two distinct planes exist: a metadata platform holding tenant metadata (in the tenant's home region) and a back-end capacity platform doing compute and storing customer data (in the capacity region).
Authentication is delegated entirely to Microsoft Entra ID, including support for conditional access policies and service principals.

Data residency is controlled by where the tenant's metadata cluster and workspace capacities are placed, with Multi-Geo capacities as the mechanism for storing/processing data outside the home region.
Workspaces are the primary OneLake security boundary, with item-level permissions layered on top for finer-grained access.

claims.text: Fabric's platform infrastructure separates a metadata platform, which stores tenant metadata (including customer data) in the tenant's home region, from a back-end capacity platform, which performs compute operations and stores customer data in the capacity's region.

Because Fabric is delivered as SaaS built on Azure rather than PaaS, many security, compliance, and governance controls are built into the platform itself and require little or no separate setup by the customer, unlike traditional PaaS data products.

Fabric authenticates users and service principals exclusively through Microsoft Entra ID, which issues access tokens that Fabric then uses to perform operations in the context of that identity, including support for Entra conditional access policies such as multifactor authentication and Intune device enrollment requirements.

All Fabric permissions are stored centrally in the metadata platform, and for performance Fabric can encapsulate authorization decisions into signed tokens that are issued only by the back-end capacity platform and bundle the access token with authorization information and metadata.

A tenant's data residency is determined by its home metadata platform cluster region plus the region(s) of the capacities its workspaces run on; customers can additionally provision Multi-Geo capacities so compute and storage, including OneLake, run in a different geography than the tenant's home metadata region.

All Fabric data stores are encrypted at rest with Microsoft-managed keys by default, data is never persisted unencrypted (though it may be processed unencrypted in memory), and customers can optionally bring their own Azure Key Vault keys via workspace customer-managed keys to encrypt specific workspaces.

Data in transit between Microsoft services, and for inbound Fabric traffic, is encrypted with at least TLS 1.2 and negotiates up to TLS 1.3 where possible; outbound Fabric communication to customer-owned infrastructure now requires TLS 1.2 or later, and TLS 1.0/1.1 are no longer supported.

OneLake is automatically provisioned for every Fabric tenant and is API/SDK-compatible with Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, so existing ADLS Gen2 tooling such as Azure Databricks can work against it without modification.

Workspaces are the primary security boundary for data stored in OneLake, with access managed through workspace roles; item-level security layered on top lets an admin grant access to a single Fabric item, such as a warehouse or lakehouse, without exposing the rest of the workspace.

Fabric platform infrastructure services are multitenant with logical isolation between tenants, run only managed code (never customer-written code), and the metadata and back-end capacity platforms each sit in secured virtual networks that expose only limited endpoints while blocking direct public internet access otherwise.
